description: We are a team of Management Information Systems students from Bursa Uludağ University. Our name comes from Atatürk's words "İstikbal göklerdedir", meaning "The future is in the skies." We are excited to take on the Space Apps Challenge, learn together and create something meaningful with NASA's data
summary:
AstroSelf is a health companion that helps astronauts assess their own health when Earth is too far away to ask. In January 2026, a crew returned early from the ISS for a medical reason for the first time, and on Mars a message and its reply can take up to 44 minutes. NASA itself lists medical decision support that works without Earth as an open gap (ExMC Med07/Med10).

AstroSelf works in four steps. The astronaut logs six daily signs (heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep and mood) or imports a wearable's export file. The app compares each value first with the person's own baseline, then with Earth reference ranges and NASA-derived limits. Affected body systems light up on an interactive 3D anatomy model, and each organ panel explains how NASA's five space hazards affect it, what to do, and when to inform the flight surgeon. Offline emergency checklists, a live space-weather alert and a 30-day trend outlook support early action.

AstroSelf is a free web app (PWA) that works without internet once installed. It uses real NASA data (Inspiration4 blood values from NASA OSDR, NASA-STD-3001 radiation limits) and clearly labels all simulated data. It is a prototype, not a medical device.
details:
What it does and how it works

AstroSelf is a health companion that lets astronauts assess their own health on long missions, when Earth is too far away to ask. It works in four steps:

1. Measure: Every day the astronaut logs six signs: heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep (hours and quality on a 1–7 scale) and mood. Each field has a short "How to measure?" guide. Values can also be imported from a wearable's CSV/JSON export, with automatic unit conversion.

2. Evaluate: A rule engine compares each value first with the astronaut's own baseline (mean and spread of the first mission days), then with Earth reference ranges and NASA-derived limits. A value only turns red when the Earth reference agrees, which reduces false alarms. The result is one of four levels, from normal to "notify the flight surgeon".

3. Show: Affected body systems light up on an interactive 3D anatomy model. Tapping any spot names it down to the finger and opens a panel explaining what the organ does and how NASA's five space hazards affect it.

4. Guide: Each panel lists self-care steps and when to inform the flight surgeon, with the communication delay for the chosen environment (ISS, Orion, Moon base, Mars transit, Mars base).

Other features: offline emergency checklists (radiation storm, loss of consciousness, chest pain, cabin depressurization, severe injury, psychological crisis) with an "Earth reply in" timer; a live space-weather card (NOAA GOES proton flux and NASA DONKI) that raises a shelter alert at the NOAA S1 level; a 30-day risk outlook based on the last 14 days' trend plus cumulative radiation dose against the 600 mSv career limit and bone loss at NASA's 1–1.5% per month rate; a simulated 4-person, 180-day crew view; and a printable report for the flight surgeon.

Benefits and intended impact

AstroSelf gives the crew an early warning before small changes become emergencies, and a clear rule for when to call the flight surgeon. It addresses a gap NASA lists itself: medical decision support that works without Earth (ExMC Med07/Med10). The same approach could help other isolated crews, such as Antarctic stations or ships.

Tools and technology

HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step; Three.js for the 3D anatomy (Z-Anatomy models, CC BY-SA 4.0); Chart.js for trend charts; a Progressive Web App (manifest and service worker) so it installs from the browser and works without internet once installed; IndexedDB for on-device storage; Python scripts to convert NASA OSDR CSV files into JSON; GitHub Pages for free hosting. No special hardware: it runs on the laptops and tablets crews already use.

Creativity

Judging each astronaut against their own normal instead of one general range; finger-level 3D anatomy tied to NASA's five space hazards; environment-aware communication delays; and an explainable trend outlook instead of a black-box model.

What our team considered

Working without internet and with long communication delays; large touch targets usable with gloves and a high-contrast theme; Turkish and English interfaces; health data that stays on the device; real NASA data (Inspiration4 blood values from NASA OSDR, NASA-STD-3001 limits) with every simulated value clearly labelled; and safety: the app never gives a diagnosis or a medication dose. It is a prototype, not a medical device.
